title: MQTT, for the house
blurb: The protocol devices speak: topics, QoS, sessions, retained values and wills; Python clients; and the NATS leaf on jarvis as the house's broker.
lede: MQTT from the wire up, with the house as the example: the protocol, Python clients, and the NATS leaf on jarvis as the broker.

shift.label: The one big mental shift
shift.html:
Nothing in MQTT is addressed to anyone. A device publishes a fact to a topic; whoever cares has subscribed. There's no answer, no caller waiting, and a message nobody subscribed to is simply gone.

So for every message, ask: who needs this later, not just now (retain it, or keep a session)? What happens if it arrives twice (QoS 1)? And how will anyone know the sender died (a last will)?

plan_foot: When you finish a day, explain one of its topics out loud as if to a friend setting up their first smart plug: what the device publishes, who subscribes, and what happens when the Wi-Fi drops.

items.t: Broker, clients, topics: nobody is addressed
items.why: A device publishes to a topic on the broker; subscribers get copies. One long-lived TCP connection per client, opened by the client, so devices behind NAT need no open port.

items.t: Keepalive: PINGREQ, and dead after 1.5×
items.why: The client promises to be heard from every N seconds. Silence for 1.5 × N and the broker drops it and publishes its will.

items.t: Topic levels and the wildcards + and #
items.why: + is exactly one level, # is the rest and must be last, and home/# also matches home. Wildcards only in subscriptions. No leading slash; case matters.

items.t: A naming scheme: home/<room>/<device>/<what>, commands on /set
items.why: General to specific, stable ids, data in the payload not the topic. Write the scheme down before the first device arrives.

items.t: CONNECT and CONNACK: client ID, credentials, return codes
items.why: Code 1 is "wrong protocol version" (an MQTT 5 client on a 3.1.1 broker), 4 bad password, 5 not authorised. Same client ID twice: the first is kicked off.

items.t: QoS 0, 1, 2, and the lower of publish and subscribe wins
items.why: QoS is per hop. 0 for frequent readings, 1 for commands and events with an idempotent handler, 2 rarely.

items.t: Persistent sessions: subscriptions and QoS 1 messages kept while you're away
items.why: Clean session off, a stable client ID, and QoS 1 on both ends. QoS 0 is never queued for an offline client.

items.t: Retained messages: the last value, for whoever subscribes later
items.why: One per topic. Clear it with an empty retained publish. Retain state, never events or commands.

items.t: The status pattern: retained will "offline", retained birth "online"
items.why: The will fires only on an unclean disconnect, so publish "offline" yourself before a clean one.

items.t: Payloads: units, UTC timestamps, one format per topic
items.why: The broker sees bytes. Decode defensively: one bad message costs a log line, not the subscriber.

items.t: Commands and state are different topics
items.why: .../set ON is a wish; ... ON (retained) is the device's report. Send the target state, never "toggle".

checks.t: I can say which of home/kitchen, home/kitchen/temp and /home/kitchen match home/# and home/+
I can explain why a QoS 1 command can arrive twice, and make the handler not care
I can draw the online/offline pattern with will, birth and a clean shutdown
I can say why a retained command is a bug

items.t: paho-mqtt 2: CallbackAPIVersion.VERSION2, subscribe in on_connect
items.why: Old examples use the version 1 callbacks. Subscribing in on_connect means every reconnect subscribes again.

items.t: The loop thread runs your callbacks and the keepalive
items.why: A slow callback stops both. Hand slow work to a queue and a worker.

items.t: aiomqtt: async for message in client.messages
items.why: No callbacks, no threads. message.topic.matches() applies the wildcard rules; message.payload is bytes.

items.t: Your own reconnect loop, with backoff, subscribing each time
items.why: aiomqtt raises MqttError and stops; you decide how to come back.

items.t: One MQTT client in the FastAPI lifespan, shared by routes
items.why: Never a connection per HTTP request.

items.t: Command, then wait for the confirmed state
items.why: Show "not confirmed" when the state topic doesn't follow within a few seconds.

items.t: Request/response on 3.1.1: reply topic and id in the payload
items.why: Subscribe to the reply topic before sending; always time out. Between your own programs, use NATS request/reply.

items.t: Debounce, dedupe, publish on change plus a heartbeat
items.why: Last acted-on value per topic; a reading at least every few minutes even when nothing changes.

items.t: Tests against a throwaway local broker
items.why: Keep the handler a plain function of (topic, payload); test reconnects and bad payloads against a real broker.

items.t: Build one: the Mac's load on home/mac/load
items.why: aiomqtt, a retained status with a will, publish on change plus a heartbeat, and a reconnect loop. Run it against a local broker; kill the Wi-Fi and check it comes back.

checks.t: I can say why a paho client that subscribed right after connect() goes deaf after a Wi-Fi blip
I can write an aiomqtt reconnect loop from memory
I can say what a blocking call in a message handler does to the connection

items.t: The mqtt block on jarvis, with js_domain: home
items.why: MQTT state lives in JetStream; keeping it in the home domain keeps the house working without the internet. The mqtt listener has its own host: 0.0.0.0 unless set.

items.t: Topics become subjects: / to ., . to //, # to two subscriptions
items.why: So a NATS program on the VPS can subscribe to what a device publishes at home.

items.t: From a NATS client, MQTT subscribers get QoS 0
items.why: Commands that must wait for an offline device go over MQTT at QoS 1, not nats pub.

items.t: A login per device, limited to its own topics
items.why: allowed_connection_types: ["MQTT"] and permissions on the converted subjects. Plan how today's login-free local programs keep working.

items.t: 1883 on the home network only, never forwarded
items.why: Outside the house: the tailnet, or NATS through the hub. The tailnet is shared with friends, so it isn't a login.

items.t: Read Tasmota, ESPHome and Zigbee2MQTT topics
items.why: cmnd/stat/tele; <prefix>/status; zigbee2mqtt/<name> and /set. Every one does will and birth.

items.t: Home Assistant discovery: retained config under homeassistant/
items.why: Republish on homeassistant/status online; clear an old one with an empty retained message.

items.t: Watch the broker first: mosquitto_sub -t '#' -v, nats sub 'home.>'
items.why: If the message shows there, the fault is the subscriber; if not, the publisher or its permissions.

items.t: Symptoms to causes: ID fights, lost subscriptions, stale retained values
items.why: The table in the lesson covers most of what will go wrong.

items.t: Dry run: a NATS server with MQTT on the Mac
items.why: nats-server -js with an mqtt block and two users with permissions. Connect the build from day 2 as one of them; check the other can't publish to its topics. Only then plan the change to pinix.

checks.t: I can write the subscribe permissions a device needs for home/kitchen/fridge/# on NATS
I can say why a command sent with nats pub to a sleeping device is lost
Given "it connects, then drops every few seconds", I name the cause first
